15.1.b:
First, what these fractures are and who gets them.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is a periprosthetic fracture?"
- "A fracture next to an implant, **during** surgery or **after** it."
- "Every system asks two questions: is the implant **stable**, and is the **bone** good?"
- "Stable → fix the fracture; loose → revise the implant."

### Definition and Significance
The definition is short; the aims follow from it.
- At the hip it hits the acetabulum or femur; at the knee, femur, tibia or patella
- It is rising, because younger, active patients get more arthroplasties
[[FIG: Fig 15.1 · 15.1
- Treatment aims at two things: **fracture union** and **implant stability**
- Alignment and function are restored as well

### Common Logic of Hip and Knee Classifications
Hip and knee systems differ in names, but they ask the same questions.

| Question | Hip | Knee |
|---|---|---|
| Where is it? | Vancouver A · B · C | Su level · Felix I–IV |
| Is the implant fixed? | **B1** fixed vs **B2** loose | Rorabeck I–II vs **III** · Felix A vs B |
| Is the bone good? | **B2** good vs **B3** poor | Ortiguera IIIa vs IIIb |

MEMORY HOOK — steady stays, loose leaves
- A steady stem stays: fix the bone. A loose stem leaves: revise it.

### Risk Factors
Risk comes from the patient's bone and from what the surgeon does to it.

#### Patient and Implant Factors
| Patient | Implant and technique |
|---|---|
| Age · **female sex** · **osteoporosis** · RA (rheumatoid arthritis) | **Osteolysis** and loosening |
| **Paget** disease · DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip) | **Cementless** stem: more fractures, especially in elderly women |
| Abnormal femoral shape: difficult insertion | Extensive instrumentation · **revision**: bone loss, stress risers, cement removal |

- Osteoporotic bone and rheumatoid disease are the classic weak hosts
[[FIG: Fig 15.2 · 15.1

#### Patient Assessment
- Pain before the fall points to **loosening** or osteolysis → 14 Aseptic loosening
- Pain and stiffness since surgery need an **infection** work-up → 11 Painful arthroplasty
- Ask whether the patient walked before the fracture
- Examine nerves and vessels, and get the implant records: type, company, size

Then think ahead to the implant.
- A neurological disorder needs a large head, tripolar or **dual mobility** → 13 Instability

### Intraoperative Femoral Fractures
Some fractures are made by the surgeon, so they are the ones we can prevent.

#### Incidence
- Intra-operative femoral fractures complicate **1.7%** of primaries (Campbell)
- They rise to **12%** of revisions
- A cementless press-fit stem (oversized) fractures more than a cemented one (smaller than the broach)
- An undisplaced crack along the stem is easy to miss
[[FIG: Fig 15.3 · 15.1

#### Mechanisms
Each step adds a twisting or wedging force.

| Step | Trigger |
|---|---|
| **Neck cut** | too high: keep it one fingerbreadth above the lesser trochanter · head pulled out before cutting a long neck |
| **Reaming, broaching** | rigid reamer or rasp · hurried hammering in osteoporotic bone · press-fit stem bigger than the canal: rasped 6, size 7 forced |
| **Stem length** | long straight stem against the **anterior bow** |
| **Reduction** | trial or final reduction twisting the femur |
| **Revision** | poor bone stock · cement removal · impaction grafting |

#### Prevention
- Expose well, template, and trial first; never force osteoporotic bone
[[FIG: Fig 15.4 · 15.1
- A difficult exposure, such as **protrusio**, needs soft-tissue release before any step
- In a stiff hip, cut the neck before dislocating
- Resistance at dislocation → release more capsule and resect rim osteophytes first
- Direct dislocation of an osteoporotic femur breaks it, so release adequately first

During broaching, two habits help.
- Look for a crack after each broach
- An implant bigger than the last broach wedges the femur apart, so stop and check

#### The Difficult Femur
- A stuck revision stem needs an **ETO** (extended trochanteric osteotomy)
[[FIG: Fig 15.5 · 15.1
- A controlled cut beats an uncontrolled fracture
- A varus femur reamed in varus perforates; an ETO allows **neutral reaming**
- The ETO itself cracks at a square corner, a deflected saw or an unreleased pseudocapsule
- A fragile femur gets a **distal cerclage** before reaming, so it does not shatter
[[FIG: Fig 15.6 · 15.1
- Do it also in a primary with a long stem: it is the most forgotten step
- No cables → a **double-wire cerclage**

After failed fixation, two more traps lie in the canal.
- Cortical pieces block the canal; rasps remove only cancellous bone, so use a **high-speed burr**
- The stem passes the last **screw hole** by **2 cortical diameters**, about 4 cm (Prof Gobba)
[[FIG: Fig 15.7 · 15.1
- A stem tip at the hole is a stress riser that fractures

CLINICAL PEARL — found a crack?
- **Calcar split**: stem out, cable, reinsert; still unstable → bypass to the diaphysis
- Expose the crack to its end, broach in place; cable it, plus **one cable distal**; trial one size smaller
- Suspected fracture → film in theatre or at once: undisplaced distal cracks are missed

### Postoperative Femoral Fractures
Most come years later, usually after a low-energy fall.

#### Incidence and Timing
- They follow **1%** of primaries and **4%** of revisions (Prof Kassem)
- Mean time to fracture: **7.3 years** (Swedish register), **8.1 years** (Mayo Clinic)
- High-energy injury causes **<10%** of them (Campbell)

#### Pathomechanics
- The stem tip is a **stress riser**: a stiff stem in flexible bone
- So late fractures happen there
- Osteolysis and loosening add risk; a **varus** stem bends the lateral cortex more
- Major trauma and extreme movement in a non-compliant patient add risk

#### Prevention
- Avoid cortical defects and malalignment
- Serial films catch osteolysis before it breaks
- "Catch the patient before he catches you": loosening seen early is a fracture prevented
- Prevention is the best treatment, and the exam answer
- Treat **osteoporosis** and fall risk, because most late fractures follow a simple fall

15.2.b:
Classification turns the fracture's place, the stem and the bone into one letter.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you classify a periprosthetic femoral fracture?"
- "**Vancouver**: A trochanters, B around the stem, C below it; then stem stability, then bone."
- "**B1** stable: fix · **B2** loose, good bone: revise · **B3** loose, poor bone: rebuild."
- "Intra-operative: modified Vancouver A–C, subtypes **1 perforation, 2 crack, 3 displaced**."

### Modified Vancouver Classification (Intraoperative)
The theatre version adds a subtype, because it decides whether a cable is enough.

#### Types and Subtypes
| Type | Site |
|---|---|
| **A** | proximal metaphysis |
| **B** | diaphysis around the stem |
| **C** | distal to the stem |

- The subtypes fit **every** type: **1** perforation, **2** undisplaced crack, **3** displaced, unstable
[[FIG: Fig 15.8 · 15.2
- The type shows what is threatened; the subtype, whether a simple cable will hold

#### Treatment by Type and Subtype
| Type | Treatment by subtype (Prof Kassem) |
|---|---|
| **A** | A1 graft (head, reamings) · A2 metaphyseal cerclage · A3 cables or plate |
| **B** | B1 longer stem + graft · B2 stable: cerclage · B2 unstable, B3: longer stem + fixation ± graft |
| **C** | C1 cortical strut · C2 cerclage or plate · C3 **ORIF** (open reduction, internal fixation) |

- Type A in the course: management and an example
[[FIG: Fig 15.9 · 15.2
- A perforation is passed by the stem by **≥2 cortical diameters**, so load goes to intact bone
[[FIG: Fig 15.10 · 15.2
- In type C the stem is left alone: strut, cerclage or plate
[[FIG: Fig 15.11 · 15.2
- Case: intra-operative type B → cerclage wires + cementless modular **Wagner** stem (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 15.12 · 15.2

### Vancouver Classification (Postoperative)
After surgery, the system reads three things in order: location, stem fixation, bone stock.

#### Types
| Type | Site | Stem and bone (Campbell) |
|---|---|---|
| **A-G · A-L** | greater · lesser trochanter | — |
| **B1** | around or just below the stem | stable |
| **B2** | around or just below the stem | loose · good bone |
| **B3** | around or just below the stem | loose · poor bone: osteolysis, comminution |
| **C** | well below the stem | not involved |

- B1 shows no radiolucency, osteolysis or migration
- B2 shows radiolucency, but the bone has no comminution or loss
- Type B is the commonest and the hardest
[[FIG: Fig 15.13 · 15.2
- **UCS** (Unified Classification System) uses Vancouver logic for every joint; it differs, so know both

MEMORY HOOK — Above, By, Clear
- **A** is Above the stem (trochanters), **B** is By the stem, **C** is Clear below it.

PITFALL — is there a Vancouver D?
- Course: A, B, C only; Campbell adds **D = interprosthetic**, between hip and knee implants
- Say → "Vancouver is A–C; between two implants is **D**, with the same stability rules"

#### Distinguishing B1 from B2
- Ask about pain before the fracture, and plan a stability test in theatre
[[FIG: Fig 15.14 · 15.2

| Test | What it gives |
|---|---|
| Long AP + long lateral of the **whole femur** | fracture and stem tip |
| **AP pelvis** | offset · alone, it misses the stem tip |
| **CT** | stock, extension, seating, wear, comminution |
| Bone scan | false positives after a fracture |

- Plain films come first; never plan on CT alone
- The AP pelvis shows both hips, so the other side guides templating
- The course films: AP pelvis and long femoral views to the knee (figure → 05)
- CT and 3D reconstruction before the revision
[[FIG: Fig 15.15 · 15.2

The classroom case trains the order of questions.
- A woman of 75 years, a THA of 7 years, a fracture around the stem
[[FIG: Fig 15.16 · 15.2
- Comminution alone does not make B3; an unstable stem with good bone is **B2**

EXAM PEARL — B1 on film, B2 at surgery
- The fracture breaks the fixation interface, so films miss it: test the stem in theatre
- Many "B1" prove **B2**; broken **cement mantle**, lucent lines or lytic bone mean loose (Miller)
- A cement fracture with lucent lines → revise; an intact, fixed stem → fixation only

### Level-Based Classifications
Older systems give the level only, so they cannot choose a treatment.
- The Handbook ("American Academy") grades types **1–5** by level, with no stem stability

| Type | Level |
|---|---|
| **1 · 2** | above · opposite the lesser trochanter: proximal third of the stem |
| **3** | opposite the middle third · non-comminuted |
| **4** | opposite the lower third · comminuted |
| **5** | distal to the tip |

- **Johansson** and **Bethea** are older level systems with the same flaw
- So in the viva, lead with **Vancouver**

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Where → loose? → bone · B1 fix, B2 revise, B3 rebuild · perforation → bypass 2 cortices**

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you treat a Vancouver B fracture?"
- "**Loose stem + fracture = revision**, because a plate cannot hold around a moving stem."
- "B1: **locking plate** + cables overlapping the stem · B2: **long diaphyseal stem**."
- "B3: long stem + graft, or **proximal femoral replacement** · C: plate, the stem stays."

### Preoperative Preparation
A revision is a big operation, so the patient and the joint are checked first.

#### Timing and Medical Fitness
- A fracture is not postponed a week, unless unfit for both general and spinal anaesthesia
- Gather a **multidisciplinary team**: neurology, cardiology, anaesthesia, ICU (intensive care unit)
- Uncontrolled **diabetes** (glucose ≈400) means postpone; **anticoagulants** matter too
- Some anaesthetists accept glucose up to 300; the internist corrects it acutely

#### Excluding Infection
- Rule out **infection**: cultures always, and a **spacer** on standby → 12 PJI
- Alpha-defensin is costly, so keep it for a dilemma; leukocyte esterase also confirms
- Frozen section needs in-hospital expertise, which is often lacking

#### Consent and Planning
- Tell the family everything; one consent form per operation lists all its complications
- Keep a personal planning **checklist**, and add to it with every patient

### Vancouver Type A Fractures
A trochanter fracture matters because the abductors pull on it.

#### Indications for Fixation
- Undisplaced → **conservative**
- **A-L** stays conservative, unless the **calcar** goes and loosens the stem
- Displaced **≥2 cm** → **cerclage wires**, a plate or a **claw plate** (Prof Kassem)
[[FIG: Fig 15.17 · 15.3

#### Greater Trochanter
- **A-G** is fixed to keep **abductor** function, because non-union brings a limp and instability
[[FIG: Fig 15.18 · 15.3
- A **figure-of-eight** cerclage holds the trochanter well
[[FIG: Fig 15.19 · 15.3
- An **atraumatic** GT (greater trochanter) fracture means **osteolysis** → graft
- A massive lytic defect → no ORIF

### Vancouver Type B Fractures
Here the stem decides everything: kept and plated, or replaced.

#### Treatment by Subtype
| Type | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **B1** | stem kept → **ORIF**: locking plate + proximal cables |
| **B2** | stem out → **long stem** → fracture fixation |
| **B3** | long stem + reconstruction · impossible → **proximal femoral replacement** |

- Examples: B1 plate, B2 porous-coated stem + cables, B3 tapered fluted stem
[[FIG: Fig 15.20 · 15.3

#### Type B1: Fixation around a Stable Stem
- A long locking plate: unicortical screws + cables proximally, bicortical screws distally
- Cerclage, bands or isolated screws alone fail often
- A gap between plate end and stem tip is a new **stress riser**, so **overlap** the stem
[[FIG: Fig 15.21 · 15.3

#### Type B2: Long-Stem Revision
- The plan: **revision ± fixation ± augmentation**
- Remove stem and cement (ETO if needed); insert a long **cementless** porous-coated stem
[[FIG: Fig 15.22 · 15.3
- Cementless stems are preferred: they grow into bone and fail less
- Cement removal may be easy or hard
- Bypass the fracture by **2 femoral diameters** or **4–6 cm** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- So a femur 30 mm wide needs the stem 6 cm past the fracture
- **6 cm** gives more cortical contact; a large gap leaves a less stable construct
- The stem is an **internal splint**: cables first, check stability, plate only if needed
- Plate, cable or cable–plate all cost more, and none is proven better
- Exception: a frail, low-demand patient with reconstructable bone may get ORIF

The case ended with a lesson.
- Rotating the leg at the end broke the greater trochanter: screws and cerclage
- Seen again at about 80 years, the construct held
[[FIG: Fig 15.23 · 15.3

An ETO is indicated in four settings.
- Infection, **Vancouver B2**, femoral loosening and a varus femur

#### Type B3: Reconstruction of Deficient Bone (Paprosky 3B/4)
- Options: impaction grafting, allograft–prosthesis composite, proximal femoral replacement
- How each works, and the Paprosky and AAOS defect classes → 14 Aseptic loosening

#### Instruments and Implants
- **Dual mobility cup**; cerclage cables or **Biznoska bands**; **Wagner** stem; long cemented stem
[[FIG: Fig 15.24 · 15.3
- **NCB** periprosthetic plate, a **flexible drill**, screws **3.5 and 4.5 mm** in every length
- No dual mobility → cemented snap-fit cups; also a reinforcement ring, power saw, bone graft

MEMORY HOOK — the wobbly tooth
- A plate on a loose stem is a splint on a wobbly tooth: replace the tooth instead.

### Vancouver Type C Fractures and Locking Plate Fixation
Below a well-fixed stem, the fracture is fixed and the stem left alone.

#### Indications and Problems
- A well-fixed stem means fixation, no revision: that is **B1 and C**
[[FIG: Fig 15.25 · 15.3
- Confirm the stem is stable, because an unrecognised loose stem is a **B2**
- Problems: the stem and cement block screws; healing is poor; bone is missing

#### Construct Principles
- Principles: **relative stability**, a long spanning plate, minimally invasive
[[FIG: Fig 15.26 · 15.3
- Distally **bicortical** screws; beside the stem **cables** or **unicortical** screws
[[FIG: Fig 15.27 · 15.3
- **Overlap the stem**, so no unprotected bone lies between implant tips
- The overlap is at least **2 cortical diameters** (Prof Kassem)

The goals follow.
- Stable fixation, soft tissue kept on the fragments, and restored length, offset, rotation

#### Fixation Devices
- Periprosthetic locking screws, variable-angle plates, trochanteric attachment devices
[[FIG: Fig 15.28 · 15.3
- Multi-plane devices; a positioning pin guides the cable system
- **Proximal femoral hook plate**, distal femoral locking plate, retrograde locked nail
[[FIG: Fig 15.29 · 15.3
- A **locking attachment plate** carries screws beside the stem
[[FIG: Fig 15.30 · 15.3
- A retrograde locked nail fixes a fracture far below the stem
[[FIG: Fig 15.31 · 15.3
- Screws from above, plus anterior and posterior screws, grip around the stem
[[FIG: Fig 15.32 · 15.3

PITFALL — does a locking plate compress?
- The Handbook says "hoop effect gives compression"; but a locking plate is an **internal fixator**
- Say → "the locking plate splints with **relative stability**; the hoop effect belongs to the **cables**"

### Periprosthetic Acetabular Fractures
The cup side breaks less often, but worse, and is probably under-recognised.

#### Risk Factors and Classification
- They are **uncommon but catastrophic**, and more common with **cementless** cups
- Intra-operative ones follow **0.4%** of primaries, all uncemented, mostly monoblock elliptical cups (Campbell)
- Risks: **high impaction force**, revision, an elliptical or threaded cup
[[FIG: Fig 15.33 · 15.3

#### Timing and Medical Fitness
- A fracture is not postponed a week, unless unfit for both general and spinal anaesthesia
- Gather a **multidisciplinary team**: neurology, cardiology, anaesthesia, ICU (intensive care unit)
- Uncontrolled **diabetes** (glucose ≈400) means postpone; **anticoagulants** matter too
- Some anaesthetists accept glucose up to 300; the internist corrects it acutely

#### Excluding Infection
- Rule out **infection**: cultures always, and a **spacer** on standby → 12 PJI
- Alpha-defensin is costly, so keep it for a dilemma; leukocyte esterase also confirms
- Frozen section needs in-hospital expertise, which is often lacking

#### Consent and Planning
- Tell the family everything; one consent form per operation lists all its complications
- Keep a personal planning **checklist**, and add to it with every patient

#### Type B2: Long-Stem Revision

15.4.t: Periprosthetic Femoral Fractures after Total Knee Arthroplasty
15.4.b:
The knee asks the same two questions, starting just above the femoral component.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "classify and treat a supracondylar fracture above a TKA."
- "Commonest TKA fracture, **0.3–2%**, at the top of the anterior flange: notching, osteoporosis."
- "**Lewis–Rorabeck**: I undisplaced stable · II displaced stable · III **loose**, whatever the displacement."
- "Stable → **plate** or **retrograde nail** · loose → **revision** · poor elderly bone → distal femoral replacement."

### Epidemiology and Pathogenesis
The anterior flange and a notched cortex make the supracondylar femur the weak spot.

#### Incidence
- The **supracondylar femur** is the commonest site: **0.3–2%** (Campbell)
- The Handbook quotes ≈3%, mostly in the first 2–4 years
- The patella breaks in **<1%**; the tibia is uncommon

#### Anterior Flange and Notching
- The **anterior flange** top, or an extended component, is a stress riser on weak supracondylar bone
- **Notching** is a classic but disputed risk factor; its data → 10 TKA radiographs (Anterior Notching)
- A femoral entry point too anterior notches, and limits flexion with recurvatum (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 15.41 · 15.4

#### Risk Factors and Investigations
- Risks: notching, **osteoporosis**, RA, steroids, female sex, revision, neurologic disease
- Get injury films and old films (± CT): **component fixation** decides fixation or revision
- Loose means pain before injury, progressive **lucent lines**, or position change on old films
- On routine films, most surgeons check only for notching

### Classification Systems
Three systems: the first answers "loose?", the second "how low?", the third only "how displaced?".

| System | Basis | Types |
|---|---|---|
| **Lewis–Rorabeck** | displacement + component | I <5 mm, fixed · II >5 mm, fixed (A simple, B comminuted) · III loose |
| **Su** | level vs the proximal flange border | I above · II starts at the border, runs up · III extends distal to it |
| **Neer** | displacement only, low yield | 1 <1 cm · 2 >1 cm · 3 >1 cm + comminution |

- **Lewis–Rorabeck** is the most important: type III is loose regardless of displacement (Rockwood)
[[FIG: Fig 15.42 · 15.4
- **Su** I–II → nail or plate; III (low) → locking plate or revision
- None grades **bone stock**, which decides revision or distal femoral replacement

MEMORY HOOK — Rorabeck III, the rule-breaker
- Rorabeck III ignores the drama: a hairline crack with a loose component still means revision.

### Prevention
Prevention starts with old hardware and ends with careful cuts.

#### Previous Hardware
- Old hardware: remove, wait **≥3 months**; or a **long stem** in one session (Handbook)

#### Bone Cuts
- Screw holes are stress risers; centre the cuts; no **eccentric box** in PS or CCK
- A CR design needs no box, so more bone is kept
- **Never notch**; if forced or found → stem + protected weight bearing
- An **undersized** femur notches the cortex and can fracture on impaction (Prof Abdel Karim)
- The **angel wing** checks the anterior cut before it is made (Prof Shokry)
[[FIG: Fig 15.43 · 15.4
- Laminar spreaders crush osteoporotic bone, so place them at the rim
- An intra-operative fracture is fixed in the same sitting

### Management
The fixation question picks the treatment, as at the hip.

#### Treatment by Lewis–Rorabeck Type
| Lewis–Rorabeck | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **I** (<5 mm, stable) | conservative · brace; fixation not mandatory |
| **II** (>5 mm, stable) | fixation: locking plate or retrograde nail |
| **III** (loose) | revision: long stem · **distal femoral replacement** (megaprosthesis) |

- The Handbook gives IIA a regular plate, IIB a locking plate
- But non-locked plates collapse into varus (Rockwood)
- Stable → a premolded supracondylar locking plate; submuscular gives fewer non-unions (Miller)
- A megaprosthesis also fits when fixation is impossible: severe comminution, failed fixation, a closed box

#### Plate versus Nail
- Locked plate and retrograde nail give similar results; non-union ≈**9%** (Rockwood)
[[FIG: Fig 15.44 · 15.4

| Choice | When |
|---|---|
| **Retrograde nail** | CR or open-box PS · a closed box that can be opened · distal fragment takes locking screws |
| **Burr or antegrade nail** | closed box, narrow notch, stemmed implant: **high-speed burr** |
| **Plate** | very distal, comminuted, osteoporotic · indirect reduction, early motion |

#### Outcomes and Revision
- Nails: 13 fractures, **11 (85%)** healed at a mean 16 weeks
- Weak bone gets a hinged brace
- Loose femur, or fracture at the fixation surface → diaphyseal **long stem** ± strut allograft

#### Elderly Patients
- Old age carries a high 1-year mortality
- Comminuted osteoporotic bone → **distal femoral replacement**, so immediate weight bearing
- Severe osteoporosis → **allograft-prosthetic composite**: 9 of 10 united (Campbell)

PITFALL — fixing a loose component
- A plate or nail around a loose femoral component fails, whatever the displacement
- Say → "**I check fixation on old films first: loose = Rorabeck III = revision**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Flange top · notch disputed · Rorabeck I brace, II plate/nail, III revise · old + poor bone = DFR**

15.5.t: Tibial and Patellar Fractures after Total Knee Arthroplasty
15.5.b:
Below the joint line the same logic holds; the patella adds a question: does the extensor work?

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "classify tibial and patellar fractures around a TKA."
- "Tibia: **Felix** I plateau, II stem, III distal, IV tubercle; A fixed, B loose, C intra-operative."
- "Patella: extensor mechanism and button fixation decide: **Ortiguera–Berry** I, II, III."
- "Intact extensor, stable button → **conservative** · loose → excise · extensor disrupted → fix."

### Felix Classification of Tibial Fractures
Felix grades location, implant stability and timing in one code.

#### Types
| Type | Location | Subtype |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | tibial plateau | **A** component fixed |
| **II** | around the stem (metaphyseal) | **B** component loose |
| **III** | distal to the stem | **C** intra-operative |
| **IV** | tibial tubercle | — |

- Tibial fractures are much rarer than femoral ones (Rockwood)
[[FIG: Fig 15.45 · 15.5
- Type I (plateau) often comes with a loose component and varus malalignment

#### Management
- Fixed and undisplaced → **conservative**; fixed and displaced → **fixation**
- The pattern picks the device: a plate, or screws alone
- Loose → **long-stem revision**, plus fixation of the fracture

#### Special Situations
- A **tubercle** fracture threatens the extensor → tension band; failed → allograft or mesh augment
- Cerclage or screws also fix the tubercle
- Intra-operative (C), from a trial or stem impaction → a stem bypassing the fracture
- Gunshot case: **offset stem** + proximal screws
[[FIG: Fig 15.46 · 15.5

### Classification of Patellar Fractures
The patella is graded by the extensor, the button and the bone.

#### Ortiguera–Berry and Goldberg Types
| Ortiguera–Berry | Extensor | Button | Bone stock |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | intact | well fixed | — |
| **II** | disrupted | fixed or loose | — |
| **IIIa** | intact | loose | reasonable |
| **IIIb** | intact | loose | poor |

- **Ortiguera–Berry** is the most used; Campbell gives the same types without the eponym
- **Goldberg** (Handbook): 1 peripheral · 2 fixation or extensor · 3 inferior pole · 4 fracture-dislocation

#### Risk Factors
- Risks: excess resection, **lateral release**, maltracking, raised joint line, flexion >**115°**
- A joint line raised **>8 mm** makes a patella baja, which can fracture
- Keep total patellar thickness **20–23 mm**, with residual bone **≥12–13 mm** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- A thin patella breaks at cementing or through the peg holes; drill with a stopper
- Trauma, PMMA heat necrosis, revision and a large central peg add risk
- Many are **asymptomatic**, found on routine films

### Management of Patellar Fractures
The straight-leg raise tells you whether to operate.

#### Treatment by Type
| Situation (Goldberg) | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **1** · extensor and fixation intact | cylinder cast or immobiliser, 6 weeks |
| **2** · extensor disrupted, button fixed | fixation · transverse: tension band + retinacular repair |
| **2** · button loose | fixation + revision, or excision |
| **3B** · tendon intact | conservative |
| **3A** · tendon torn | partial patellectomy + repair |

- No **straight-leg raise** means a disrupted extensor, so operate
- A loose button is excised, not replaced; poor bone is left unresurfaced (**patelloplasty**)
- Comminution and poor bone → patellectomy + extensor repair

And surgery carries a price.
- Operated types II–III have up to **50%** complications: non-union, implant failure (Campbell)

#### Clinical Example: Comminuted Patella
- A fall at 9 months crushed the patella, extensor intact: fragments out (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 15.47 · 15.5
- No augmentation device in Egypt; at 4 and 3.5 years, small remnant, normal gait

MEMORY HOOK — the leg-raise test
- If the leg lifts straight, the knife stays in the drawer: intact extensor, stable button, no operation.

PITFALL — operating on every patellar fracture
- Patellar fixation often fails; an intact extensor usually does well in a cast
- Say → "**straight-leg raise intact and button stable → non-operative**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Felix I–IV + A/B/C · Ortiguera I fixed, II extensor, III loose · SLR decides · 50% complications if operated**
